fitnessSpec.hiking: ~6 miles RT with 2,900 ft gain; roughly 2-3 hrs car-to-Kangaroo Pass, plus ~1 hr pass-to-summit each way
fitnessSpec.packWeight: light day pack - water, layers, helmet; no technical rack required for the standard line though some parties carry a rope for the low-5th-class moves near the top

partner_requirements.approachTime: ~2-3 hours from the car to Kangaroo Pass (6,671 ft), then roughly another hour to the summit
requiredSkills: route-finding on a boot path/cairned ridge with multiple braided options
comfort with exposure on the summit gully crux
loose rock/rockfall awareness for parties above/below
partner_requirements.experienceLevel: Solid Class 3-4 scrambling experience with comfort on loose, exposed terrain; not a beginner's first scramble given the crux gully and summit exposure

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Mid-summer to early fall (July-September), once seasonal snow has cleared the approach to Kangaroo Pass and the summit gully

July.reason: within the best-season window; approach and gully typically snow-free, dry rock

June.reason: before the best-season window; lingering snowpack on the approach and in the summit gully adds difficulty and consequence beyond the class 3-4 rating

August.reason: peak of the best-season window; most stable, driest conditions, though afternoon thunderstorms are a known hazard

October.reason: outside the best-season window; larch season draws more traffic to the Washington Pass corridor, but early snow/ice on the approach and gully becomes a real possibility

September.reason: still within the best-season window; cooler, stable weather but shorter daylight and possible early-season snow late in the month

before.approach: Park at the large paved turnout at the first hairpin turn on SR-20 (North Cascades Highway), about 1 mile east of the Washington Pass summit (roughly 5,160 ft elevation). There's no formal trailhead sign or numbered trail here — the route to Kangaroo Pass is an unmaintained but well-cairned climbers' path on Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest land along the edge of the Lake Chelan-Sawtooth Wilderness. From the pullout, head south/southeast toward the base of the large talus slope just south of Spire Gulch (below the north side of Kangaroo Temple). Pick up the boot path skirting the bottom of the talus field and follow cairns carefully — this lower boulder/talus band is the trickiest route-finding on the approach, especially if snow-covered early in the season. The tread firms up into a distinct, easy-to-follow cairned trail once you're in the upper basin. Continue up mixed talus, boulders, and open slope to Kangaroo Pass (6,671 ft), gaining about 1,500 ft over roughly 1.5 miles — typically 1 to 1.5 hours. A small tarn just below the pass is the only reliable water source on the approach; there is none higher, so top off here. Expect lingering snow from about 5,800 ft up to the pass into early-mid summer, depending on the year — an ice axe and/or microspikes are worth carrying into July. At Kangaroo Pass, leave the boot path and turn northeast onto Wallaby Peak's southwest ridge. A faint climbers' trail continues briefly then disappears on rock; stay on or near the ridge crest, weaving between its north and south sides across mixed rock, scree, and grassy benches. At about 7,400 ft, swing around onto the south flank into the south-facing summit gully. This gully is moderately steep with notable loose rock and scree — wear a helmet, especially with more than one person in the party, since climbers above can kick debris down onto those below; some parties pick a short Class 3 line on the gully's margins to avoid the worst of the scree. Near the top of the gully, exit left (northeast) for the short final scramble to the true summit. Total distance is about 3.0 miles one-way (6.0 mi / ~2,900 ft round trip, or 9.7 km); budget roughly 2 hours car-to-pass and another hour pass-to-summit.

waypoints.name: SR-20 Hairpin Pullout
waypoints.note: Large paved pullout at the hairpin turn on the North Cascades Highway just east of Washington Pass crest; no signed trailhead — find the boot path into the timber/boulder field on the uphill side. Northwest Forest Pass required.
waypoints.directions: Drive the North Cascades Highway (SR-20) to the first hairpin turn about a mile east of the Washington Pass summit and park in the large paved turnout on the south side of the road, around 5,160 ft. Nothing here is signed as a trailhead; the boot path starts on the uphill side of the pullout, into the timber and boulders. SR-20 is gated for winter from roughly early December to mid or late April, so check the WSDOT pass report in the shoulder seasons, and display a Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass.

waypoints.name: Boulder Field / Snowline
waypoints.note: Cairns mark the climbers' path up through timber and talus to about 5,800 ft, where the route commonly meets lingering snowpack well into summer.
waypoints.directions: From the pullout head south and southeast toward the foot of the large talus slope just south of Spire Gulch, below the north side of Kangaroo Temple. Pick up the boot path skirting the bottom of the talus and follow the cairns carefully: this lower boulder and talus band is the trickiest route-finding on the whole approach, and it is considerably worse when snow covers the tread early in the season. Around 5,800 ft you reach the level where snowpack commonly lingers well into summer.

waypoints.name: Kangaroo Pass
waypoints.note: Gain the crest of Kangaroo Ridge here between Kangaroo Temple and Wallaby Peak, about 1,500 ft above the trailhead; leave the approach path and turn east onto Wallaby's southwest ridge.
waypoints.directions: Above the boulder band the tread firms up into a distinct, easy-to-follow cairned trail through the upper basin. Keep climbing mixed talus, boulders and open slope to the crest of Kangaroo Ridge at Kangaroo Pass, 6,671 ft, roughly 1,500 ft of gain from the car in about 1 to 1.5 hours. A small tarn just below the pass is the only reliable water on the route and there is none higher, so fill up here. Expect snow on this stretch into early or mid summer depending on the year, and carry an ice axe or microspikes into July.

waypoints.name: 7,400 ft Ridge-to-Face Swing
waypoints.note: The southwest ridge narrows here; step off the crest and traverse onto the south-facing flank to reach the summit gully — boot tracks are sparse and easy to lose in poor visibility.
waypoints.directions: Leave the boot path at the pass and gain Wallaby's southwest ridge. A faint climbers' trail runs a short way and then disappears on rock, so the rest is route-finding: stay on or near the crest, weaving between its north and south sides across mixed rock, scree and grassy benches, about 530 ft of gain to an access notch near 7,200 ft. The short section between that notch and about 7,400 ft is the technical crux of the route and holds a corniced snow arete into late spring, where an axe and light crampons are commonly used.

waypoints.name: South-Facing Summit Gully
waypoints.note: Loose talus and scree gully gains the final several hundred feet; Class 3 rock on either side avoids the worst scree, and this same gully is the descent line — watch for rockfall from parties above.
waypoints.directions: Where the crest narrows near 7,400 ft, step off it and traverse onto the south-facing flank to reach the summit gully. Boot tracks are sparse here and easy to lose in poor visibility. The gully is moderately steep with a great deal of loose rock and scree, so wear a helmet and avoid stacking the party directly above one another, since anyone higher will kick debris onto anyone below. Many parties take a short Class 3 line on the more solid rock at the gully's margins rather than wading up the scree.

waypoints.name: Wallaby Peak
waypoints.note: True summit of Wallaby Peak on Kangaroo Ridge (7,995 ft); first climbed by Fred and Helmy Beckey with Walt Varney on June 17, 1942.
waypoints.directions: Climb the gully for the final several hundred feet, then near its top exit left, to the northeast, for the short scramble to the true summit at 7,995 ft. The slabs just below the summit block stay exposed and are genuinely committing when wet or snow-covered, even in midsummer. This same gully is the descent line, downclimbed one at a time.

approach_variants.name: Kangaroo Pass from the highway hairpin
approach_variants.notes: Park in the large paved turnout at the first hairpin turn about a mile east of the pass summit. Nothing is signed; the boot path starts on the uphill side of the pullout into timber and boulders. Head south and south-east toward the foot of the large talus slope below the big tower to the north, pick up the path skirting the bottom of the talus, and follow cairns carefully — this lower boulder band is the trickiest route-finding of the approach and is much worse under snow. Above it the tread firms into a distinct cairned trail through the upper basin to the pass. A small tarn just below the pass is the only reliable water anywhere on the route.
approach_variants.season: July to early October, and the ridge is at its best when the larches turn; the highway is gated through winter and lingering snow reaches the pass into early summer
hazards: A corniced snow arete between the access notch and about 7,400 ft into late spring
The summit gully is loose scree and rock and parties above will kick debris onto those below
The slabs just below the summit block are committing when wet or snow-covered, even in midsummer
approach_variants.baseFinding: Kangaroo Pass is the base and the big tower is the marker: it stands immediately NORTH of the pass, so at the pass you turn away from it, north-east onto the south-west ridge. A faint climbers' trail runs a short way off the pass and then dies on rock, which is normal. Stay on or very near the crest, weaving between its north and south sides across mixed rock, scree and grassy benches. The feature to find is an access notch near 7,200 ft where the crest narrows; the short stretch between that notch and about 7,400 ft is the technical crux and is where a corniced snow arete lingers into late spring. At about 7,400 ft step OFF the crest onto the south flank into the summit gully, a moderately steep runnel of loose rock and scree with cleaner class 3 rock on its margins. If you are still on the crest above 7,400 ft with the ground steepening into real climbing, you have missed the swing onto the south side. If you are descending west from the pass, you are back on the approach path to the road.

itinerary.cal: Best in a dry-summer to fall window (July-Oct); the SW gully/talus is loose and can hold snow into early summer, and larch season (late Sept-early Oct) is a popular time given light views.

days.note: From the Washington Pass hairpin pullout, a boot path climbs to Kangaroo Pass, then the route turns up the southwest ridge before cutting into a south-facing gully for the final push to the summit. The crux is route-finding and loose rock in the upper two-thirds, not sustained technical difficulty; most parties are back at the car well before dark.
days.title: Car-to-car scramble via Kangaroo Pass

schedule.label: Leave trailhead
schedule.detail: Hairpin pullout east of Washington Pass on Hwy 20; start on the boot path/cairned route.

schedule.label: Reach Kangaroo Pass (6,671 ft)
schedule.detail: Roughly 1.5 miles and 1,500 ft of gain on a rough but findable path; poles and a GPS track help.

schedule.label: Gain the southwest ridge (~7,400 ft)
schedule.detail: Traverse upward from the pass onto the ridge; some easy class 3 optional to avoid loose talus.

schedule.label: Ascend south gully to summit (7,995 ft)
schedule.detail: Loose scree/talus in the final gully makes this leg slower than the 1-hour published estimate; helmet recommended.

schedule.label: Summit
schedule.detail: Views of Kangaroo Temple, Liberty Bell, and the Washington Pass area; larches are especially good in fall.

schedule.label: Descend to trailhead
schedule.detail: Reverse the ascent route back through the gully, ridge, and pass to the car.

days.objective: Summit via the Southwest Ridge/Gully and return same day

itinerary.totalNote: A single long day car-to-car: about 6 miles round trip and 2,900 ft of gain, typically 6-9 hours depending on pace and route-finding through the loose upper gully.
